It looks like you are attempting to set the height of the `MDNavigationLayout` to the height of the parent minus the height of the top app bar (`dp(56)`). However, you're trying to set the height before the parent has been rendered and before the parent has a height.

One solution to fix this is to use a `bind` statement to bind the `height` property of the `MDNavigationLayout` to the height of the parent.
```
MDNavigationLayout:
    id: nav_layout
    elevation: 1
    size_hint_y: None
    height: self.parent.height - dp(56)
    bind(height=self.parent.height)
```
This will bind the height of the `MDNavigationLayout` to the height of the parent, so when the parent is rendered, the height of the `MDNavigationLayout` will be updated to be the height of the parent minus the height of the top app bar.

Also, you can use a clock schedule to schedule the height change after the parent layout is rendered.
```
Clock.schedule_once(lambda dt: self.height = self.parent.height - dp(56))
```

POS tagging is the process of assigning a part-of-speech (such as noun, verb, adjective, etc) to each word in a sentence.

* Rule-based tagger:
	+ Uses hand-coded rules to assign tags to words.
	+ Uses a lexicon to obtain a list of candidate tags and then uses rules to discard incorrect tags.
	+ Has a 2 stage architecture:
		- First stage is a dictionary look-up procedure, which returns a set of potential tags and appropriate syntactic features for each word.
		- Second stage uses hand-coded rules to discard contextually illegitimate tags to get a single part of speech for each word.
	+ Uses contextual and morphological information to help in the disambiguation process.
	+ Requires supervised training
* Hybrid Tagger:
	+ Combines the rule-based and data-driven approaches.
	+ Uses a combination of hand-crafted rules and statistical models to predict the POS tags.
	+ Can leverage the strengths of both approaches to improve the accuracy.
	+ Typically, Hybrid tagger is the combination of rule based and stochastic tagger.
	+ Can be more accurate than either approach alone.

A program can certainly include functions and methods, but it is more accurate to say that a program is a set of instructions that a computer can execute. These instructions can take many different forms, including functions, methods, and other programming constructs like loops, conditionals, and variables.

Functions and methods are both types of subroutines that perform a specific task within a program. Functions are generally standalone procedures that take inputs and return outputs, while methods are functions that are associated with a specific object or class. However, not all programs necessarily use functions or methods - some may consist entirely of a sequence of instructions that are executed one after the other.

So, while functions and methods are important programming constructs, they are just a part of what makes up a program.
